props.title: The Man from London

sections.content: The Man from London represents Hungarian auteur Béla Tarr's penultimate film, showcasing his masterful command of slow cinema techniques. Shot in his signature black-and-white with hypnotic long takes, it adapts Georges Simenon's noir novel into a mesmerizing meditation on guilt and observation. Like Tarr's magnum opus Werckmeister Harmonies (2000), it uses stark compositions and glacial pacing to create an atmosphere of existential dread. The film follows a railway switchman who witnesses a murder and theft, drawing comparisons to Hitchcock's Rear Window (1954), but filtered through Tarr's uniquely contemplative Eastern European sensibility.

sections.content: The film's opening 12-minute shot, tracking a suitcase exchange that ends in murder, exemplifies Tarr's formal mastery. Unlike conventional noir thrillers like The Third Man (1949), Tarr strips away narrative momentum in favor of prolonged observation. His camera lingers on faces, empty corridors, and rain-slicked streets, creating a darkness that feels both physical and metaphysical. The influence of this methodical style can be seen in contemporary slow cinema directors like Lav Diaz (Norte, the End of History [2013]) and Pedro Costa (Horse Money [2014]).

Working with longtime collaborator Ágnes Hranitzky, Tarr crafts images of extraordinary power through minimal means. The film's port setting recalls Jean-Pierre Melville's Le Samouraï (1967), but where Melville emphasized sleek efficiency, Tarr finds existential weight in every gesture and glance. The performance of Miroslav Krobot as Maloin anchors the film with a heavy stillness reminiscent of Bruno Ganz in Theo Angelopoulos's Eternity and a Day (1998). sections.content: While The Man from London draws from noir traditions established in films like Double Indemnity (1944), it radically reconfigures the genre's conventions. Tarr's version of noir eschews plot mechanics for philosophical inquiry, using crime as a lens to examine moral culpability and human isolation. This approach aligns him with other art house directors who've deconstructed noir, from Andrei Tarkovsky's Stalker (1979) to Claire Denis's Bastards (2013).
